rw: Unbundling means billing separately for parts of a procedure that payers expect under one comprehensive code, which inflates payment and is treated as improper billing by insurers and regulators.

ww.Sending a bill to a patient and to the i: Sending one bill to both the patient and the insurer is duplicate billing, a different problem, and it does not split a bundled service into separate parts for extra payment.
ww.Splitting a patient's bill into payments: Splitting a bill into monthly installments is a payment plan, which is a collection arrangement and has nothing to do with how services are coded or grouped on a claim.
ww.Combining unrelated services into one co: Combining unrelated services into one code describes bundling or miscoding, the opposite direction from unbundling, which breaks apart services that belong together rather than merging them.

rw: A remittance advice or explanation of payment is sent by the payer to the provider, showing what was paid, adjusted or denied on each claim, so billers can post payments accurately.

ww.A letter to a patient that thanks him fo: A thank-you letter to a patient is a courtesy message and says nothing about how a claim was paid, so it cannot be a remittance advice, which comes from the payer.
ww.A form a patient signs to agree to treat: A consent form signed before a procedure is a clinical and legal document about treatment agreement, not a payer statement, and it has no information on claim payment or adjustments.
ww.A report on how many patients visited th: A report on monthly patient visits is an operational statistic produced by the clinic itself, while a remittance advice comes from the payer and explains the outcome of individual claims.

rw: A timely filing limit is the deadline set by a payer for submitting a claim after service, and claims sent after it are usually denied with little chance of payment.

ww.The time an insurer has to answer a phon: How long an insurer takes to answer a call is a service measure, not a filing rule, because the timely filing limit restricts the provider's claim submission window instead.
ww.The time a patient may wait in the waiti: Waiting room time is a patient satisfaction and flow measure that has no link to billing, whereas timely filing concerns how long a provider has to send a claim.
ww.The number of claims a biller may send t: A cap on claims per day would be a volume rule, but timely filing is about the calendar deadline for each claim and not how many claims a biller may send.

rw: An HSA lets people set aside pre-tax money, usually alongside a high-deductible plan, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax free, which is the account's main purpose.

ww.Saving for retirement in a fund not used: Retirement savings accounts like a 401(k) or IRA are for later income, while an HSA is meant for health costs, so a fund not used for health misses its point.
ww.Paying hospital employees wages out of a: An HSA belongs to an individual and pays that person's qualified medical expenses, not employee wages, so paying hospital workers from a special fund is not its function.
ww.Paying car insurance premiums on the car: Car insurance premiums are not qualified medical expenses, so using an HSA for them would lose its tax benefit and add penalties, which makes this a wrong use.

rw: Medicare covers most people age 65 or older and some younger people with certain disabilities or end-stage renal disease, which makes age and disability the core eligibility rules.

ww.Only active members of the military and: Military service connects families to TRICARE and veterans programs, not to Medicare, which is a federal program based on age or disability and not on military membership.
ww.Only employees of hospitals who have wor: Medicare has no rule tied to hospital employment or ten years of service; eligibility is based on age 65 or on qualifying disabilities, not on where someone works.
ww.Only people with low income, whatever th: Low income is the test for Medicaid, not Medicare, which covers people age 65 and older regardless of income, and some under 65 with disabilities, so this mixes up the two programs.

rw: Accounts receivable is the money owed to the provider for services already delivered but not yet paid by patients or payers, and it appears as an asset on the books.

ww.Money the provider owes to suppliers for: Money the provider owes to suppliers is accounts payable, a liability, so it is the mirror image of receivables and cannot be the right definition of this term.
ww.Money the provider has in the bank to sp: Cash in the bank is already collected, so it is a cash balance and not a receivable, which refers only to amounts that are still owed and unpaid.
ww.Money the provider earns from stock mark: Investment income comes from holdings in the market and is separate from patient care billing; receivables are tied to services already delivered, not to returns on stocks.

rw: Days in accounts receivable is the average time to collect payment after services are billed, so a lower number means faster cash and better billing performance for the provider.

ww.The number of days a patient stays in th: Days a patient stays in the hospital is length of stay, a clinical measure, while days in accounts receivable measures how long billed money takes to be collected.
ww.The number of days a supplier waits to b: The time a supplier waits to be paid concerns accounts payable, money the hospital owes, and the receivables measure looks at money owed to the hospital by payers and patients.
ww.The number of days between a booking and: The gap between booking and the visit is appointment lead time, an access measure, and has no relation to how many days it takes to collect payment on bills.

rw: Contribution margin per visit is 100 minus 60, which is $40, and fixed costs of $20,000 divided by $40 equal 500 visits, which is the break-even volume for the month.

ww.2,000 visits: Dividing 20,000 by 10 gives 2,000, but the contribution per visit is 100 minus 60, which is 40, so the correct divisor is 40 and not 10.
ww.200 visits: Dividing 20,000 by 100 gives 200 but ignores the 60 variable cost per visit, so it treats the whole $100 as covering fixed costs, which overstates the margin on each visit.
ww.333 visits: Dividing 20,000 by 60 gives about 333, but 60 is the variable cost and not the margin; the contribution margin is 40, so the break-even is 500 visits.

rw: Revenue minus expenses is 150,000 minus 140,000, or 10,000, and dividing by revenue of 150,000 gives about 6.7 percent, which is the operating margin for the month.

ww.About 15 percent: Operating margin is profit divided by revenue, which is 10,000 over 150,000, or about 6.7 percent, so 15 percent is far too high and matches no sensible calculation here.
ww.About 93 percent: About 93 percent is expenses divided by revenue, 140,000 over 150,000, which shows the cost ratio and not the margin; the margin is the remaining small share of about 6.7 percent.
ww.About 10 percent: Ten percent would need a surplus of $15,000 on this revenue, but the surplus is only $10,000, so the margin is lower than 10 percent at about 6.7 percent.

rw: A revenue center, such as radiology, generates income by billing patients or payers for its services, which sets it apart from support departments that only add to the cost side.

ww.A department that only costs money, such: A department that only costs money, like housekeeping, is a cost center, not a revenue center, since a revenue center brings in income from billed patient services.
ww.A department that handles patient compla: Handling patient complaints is a service function that does not generate billings, so it would be a support department and not a revenue center that earns income.
ww.A department that sets the price of ever: Setting prices is a management or finance task that sits within administration, and it does not describe a department that earns revenue by delivering billable patient services.

rw: A cost center, like housekeeping, incurs expenses to support care but does not bill patients directly, so its costs are carried by revenue centers that do earn income.

ww.A department that sets the budget for th: Setting the hospital's overall budget is a task for finance leaders and the board; a cost center is defined by its expenses and lack of billing, not by who writes budgets.
ww.A department that is closed because it c: A closed department that costs more than it earns is simply shut down, and a cost center is an operating unit that remains open and supports patient care without billing.
ww.A department that earns income by billin: A department that earns income by billing patients for care is a revenue center, the opposite of a cost center, so this option describes the wrong type of unit.

rw: A capital budget plans major, long-lasting purchases such as equipment, buildings and renovations, which are spent over several years and are separate from the day to day operating budget.

ww.A plan for the salaries and the bonuses: Executive salaries and bonuses belong in the operating budget as labor costs, whereas a capital budget covers large, long-lived purchases like equipment, so this choice mixes the two types.
ww.A plan for monthly office supplies and o: Monthly office supplies and other small purchases belong in the operating budget, since they are small, recurring expenses and not the major long-term investments that a capital budget covers.
ww.A plan for the funds that a hospital kee: A savings account kept for emergencies is a reserve or cash fund, not a capital budget, which is a plan to spend on major assets like equipment and buildings.

rw: The department spent $55,000 against a budget of $50,000, so it overspent by $5,000, and overspending on an expense is an unfavorable variance in budget reports.

ww.$5,000 favorable: Spending $55,000 against a $50,000 budget is $5,000 more than planned, and extra spending on a cost is unfavorable, so calling the variance favorable reverses its meaning.
ww.$0 and no variance: A variance is the difference between budget and actual, and these amounts differ by $5,000, so saying there is no variance ignores the clear overspending on supplies.
ww.$105,000 over budget: Adding 50,000 and 55,000 to get $105,000 mixes budget and actual; the variance is their difference of $5,000, and the overspend is not the sum of the two figures.

rw: Occupancy rate is occupied beds divided by available beds, so 150 divided by 200 equals 0.75, or 75 percent, which tells managers how fully the hospital uses its capacity.

ww.133 percent: A rate of 133 percent comes from dividing 200 by 150, which inverts the ratio; occupancy is occupied beds over total beds, and it cannot exceed 100 percent.
ww.25 percent: Twenty-five percent is the share of beds left empty, 50 out of 200; occupancy is the opposite share, the 150 occupied beds, so it is 75 percent.
ww.50 percent: Fifty percent would need only 100 occupied beds out of 200, but 150 are occupied, so the occupancy is higher than half of the available capacity.

rw: A deductible is the amount a patient pays out of pocket for covered services before the plan starts to pay, and it usually resets each year, which is its main effect.

ww.The plan pays the whole bill and the pat: If the plan paid the whole bill and the patient paid nothing, there would be no deductible; the deductible is the amount the patient must pay first before coverage starts.
ww.The patient pays a fee after the plan ha: A fee paid after the plan has covered its share describes coinsurance or a copay pattern, not a deductible, which is paid first and before the plan begins to share costs.
ww.The patient pays nothing until the end o: A deductible is not a single year-end bill; patients pay it as they receive covered care, and the plan starts paying once it has been met, not after the year has ended.

rw: Bad debt is revenue the hospital expected to collect from patients who had the ability to pay but did not, and it is written off as an uncollected balance.

ww.Care that the hospital provides at no co: Care given free to people who cannot pay is charity care, which the hospital never expected to be paid for, so it differs from bad debt, which was expected but not collected.
ww.Money the hospital owes to its suppliers: Money owed to suppliers for goods bought on credit is accounts payable, a liability, and not bad debt, which relates to unpaid patient balances owed to the hospital.
ww.Loans from a bank that the hospital has: Loans repaid early are a financing event that lowers the hospital's debt, and they have no link to bad debt, which concerns patient accounts that go unpaid.

rw: Role-based access limits each user to the information needed for the job, such as a billing clerk seeing billing data and not clinical notes, which protects privacy under the minimum necessary idea.

ww.Access granted to everyone in the hospit: Giving everyone access to all information would break privacy rules, since many staff do not need patient records, and role-based access is designed to prevent exactly that kind of open access.
ww.Access given only to the person who owns: Share ownership has nothing to do with who needs patient data; access is granted according to job duties, not according to whether someone owns shares in the organization.
ww.Access based on seniority only, so the l: Seniority alone does not justify seeing all records, because role-based access depends on job function and need, and long service does not create a need to see everything.

rw: The front desk should verify that the caller is authorized, for example through patient consent on file, before releasing any information, which protects the patient's privacy under HIPAA.

ww.Share results with anyone who sounds wor: Sharing results with a worried caller who has not been verified risks a privacy breach, because sounding worried does not prove the caller is authorized to receive health information.
ww.Share results with the caller to be poli: Being polite and saving time do not justify sharing protected information; the front desk must confirm the caller is allowed to receive it, or privacy rules may be broken.
ww.Share results with anyone who names the: Knowing a patient's name is not proof of authority, since many people can learn it, so naming the patient correctly does not allow the front desk to share results.

rw: The accepted method is to draw one line through the error, date and initial it, and then add the correct entry, so that the original text stays readable and the change is traceable.

ww.Erase the entry completely and write the: Erasing an entry completely destroys the original and hides what was recorded, which breaks record integrity; errors must stay visible and be corrected with a clear note instead.
ww.Use correction fluid to hide it so the r: Correction fluid hides the original text and makes the record look clean while removing the audit trail, which is not allowed because medical records must show what was first written.
ww.Tear out the page and write a new one wi: Tearing out a page destroys part of the legal record and concealing the change from the nurse adds to the problem, since corrections must be open, dated and attributable.

rw: Artificial intelligence helps with reading images, predicting patient risk and automating administrative work such as coding or scheduling, while clinicians keep responsibility for decisions, which makes this a realistic description of its use.

ww.Replacing all clinicians immediately, so: AI is a support tool and cannot replace all clinicians immediately; hospitals still need doctors and nurses for judgment, procedures and human care, so the claim is unrealistic.
ww.Deleting patient records that are older: Deleting records older than one year is not a use of AI and would break retention laws, which usually require records to be kept for years, not just months.
ww.Setting the price of medicines in the sh: Setting medicine prices with no regulation is not an AI function; prices are set by manufacturers, payers and laws, and AI does not exempt anyone from regulatory oversight.

rw: A CFO leads the hospital's financial strategy, budgeting, financial reporting and control of costs, making sure the organization remains financially healthy while it delivers care.

ww.Leads the care of patients and picks tre: Leading patient care and choosing treatments is the work of the chief medical officer or physicians, not the CFO, whose job covers money and financial reporting.
ww.Leads the repair and upkeep of the build: Building repair and upkeep fall under facilities or plant operations management and not under the CFO, who is concerned with finances rather than maintenance.
ww.Leads the recruiting and training of nur: Recruiting and training nurses is the role of nursing leadership or human resources, whereas the CFO focuses on budgets, financial strategy and reports.

rw: Licensure is the permission granted by a government authority, usually a state board, that allows a person to practice a profession like nursing or medicine legally.

ww.A hospital's permission to charge a high: A hospital's permission to charge more is not licensure; prices are set by the hospital or by contracts, while licensure is a government approval to practice.
ww.A discount on medical supplies for hospi: A discount on medical supplies is a purchasing benefit, perhaps through group buying, and has no relation to licensure, which authorizes a professional to practice legally.
ww.A certificate given to a patient after a: A certificate given to a patient after a course is an educational record, and licensure applies to professionals, not patients, and it comes from government and not a class.

rw: EMTALA requires hospitals with emergency rooms to give a medical screening and stabilizing treatment to anyone who arrives, regardless of ability to pay, which is why it is called an anti-dumping law.

ww.A law that gives patients the right to c: EMTALA does not give patients a free choice of any doctor nationwide; it deals with emergency screening and stabilization at hospitals with emergency departments, not with doctor selection.
ww.A law that sets the number of nurses tha: Nurse staffing ratios on wards are set by state laws or hospital policy, not by EMTALA, which instead deals with emergency screening and stabilization of arriving patients.
ww.A law that allows hospitals to turn away: EMTALA does the opposite of allowing turning away uninsured patients; it forbids refusing emergency screening or stabilization because a person lacks insurance or cannot pay.

rw: Consent must be informed, meaning the patient understands the procedure, its risks and alternatives, so a signature without any explanation may not be valid, and that is the concern.

ww.The form is valid only if it is printed: The color of the paper has no bearing on validity; what matters is that the patient understood the information and agreed voluntarily before the procedure.
ww.The patient is certain to have a bad res: Poor consent does not guarantee a bad outcome; the patient may do well, but the process was still flawed, and the legal and ethical concern remains.
ww.The insurer must pay double the usual co: Insurers do not pay double because consent was missing, and doubling the cost has no basis; the real concern is the validity of the consent and the provider's liability.

rw: Non-maleficence comes from the Latin for do no harm, meaning providers must avoid actions that injure patients, and it is one of the four core principles in medical ethics.

ww.Fair care: Fair care and the fair sharing of resources is justice, not non-maleficence, which is the duty to avoid causing harm to the patient.
ww.Patient choice: Patient choice describes autonomy, the right to decide about one's own care, which is a different ethical principle from non-maleficence, the duty not to harm.
ww.Best interest: Acting in a patient's best interest is beneficence, the duty to do good, and it is paired with but not the same as non-maleficence, which is avoiding harm.

rw: Autonomy means respecting the patient's right to make informed decisions about their own care, including refusing treatment, as long as they have the capacity to decide.

ww.Distributing care fairly among all patie: Distributing care fairly among patients is justice, one of the four ethical principles, and it is separate from autonomy, which concerns the patient's own right to choose.
ww.Acting in the best interest of the patie: Acting in the best interest even against the patient's wishes is paternalism or beneficence, and it contradicts autonomy, which requires respect for a patient's own choices.
ww.Doing no harm to the patient in any circ: Doing no harm is non-maleficence, a different principle, and the phrase in any circumstance of care is also unrealistic because some treatments carry unavoidable risks.

rw: The standard of care is the level of care that a reasonably skilled and careful provider would give in similar circumstances, and it is used to judge negligence in malpractice cases.

ww.The amount of insurance a provider must: The amount of insurance a provider holds is malpractice coverage, a financial protection, and does not define how care must be delivered or how it is judged.
ww.The number of patients a provider may tr: A daily limit on patients treated is a workload or scheduling rule, not the standard of care, which measures the quality of care and not the quantity.
ww.The lowest price at which a provider is: The lowest price a provider will accept is a pricing matter and has nothing to do with the legal measure of care quality used in negligence disputes.

rw: OSHA sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards, covering hazards in healthcare such as needlesticks, chemical exposure and bloodborne pathogens, and it inspects employers for compliance.

ww.Pays the claims of patients hurt in a ho: Paying claims of patients hurt in a hospital is done by liability insurers or compensation systems, not by OSHA, which focuses on workplace safety rules for employees.
ww.Licenses doctors and nurses to practice: Licensing doctors and nurses is the job of state licensing boards, while OSHA deals with workplace hazards, so this assigns the wrong agency to the task.
ww.Sets patient prices for hospital service: Hospital service prices are set by the hospitals and by payer contracts, not by OSHA, whose authority covers safety and health standards at work.

rw: A safety data sheet explains the hazards of a chemical and how to handle, store and respond to exposure, and employers must keep one for each hazardous product.

ww.Showing lab results to doctors after tes: Lab results shown to doctors are reports from the laboratory, whereas a safety data sheet describes chemical products, so showing results is not its purpose.
ww.Listing employees' pay and tax withholdi: Pay and tax withholding appear on payroll records, which are a finance document and have no connection to chemical hazards, the subject of a safety data sheet.
ww.Recording the dates when staff are on du: Recording when staff are on duty is a schedule or timekeeping task, not the purpose of a safety data sheet, which gives chemical safety information.

rw: A certificate of need is state approval that must be obtained before building or expanding certain health facilities or buying costly equipment, which aims to limit duplicate services and control costs.

ww.A paper a patient gets to prove that he: A paper proving a patient needs treatment would be a referral or medical order, and the CON is a state approval for facilities rather than a patient document.
ww.A document that shows a hospital has pai: Proof of tax payment is a tax clearance record and unrelated to a CON, which concerns whether the community needs a new facility or service.
ww.A license for a doctor to work in severa: A license letting doctors work across states is a multistate license or compact privilege, and a CON is not for individual doctors but for facilities.

rw: The HIPAA Privacy Rule controls who may use and disclose patients' protected health information and sets limits and patient rights, which is why providers must protect confidentiality.

ww.To count how many beds a hospital has an: Counting beds and rooms is an administrative or licensing matter, but the Privacy Rule governs how patient health information is used and shared, so it has no relation to bed counts.
ww.To require patients to share their recor: The Privacy Rule does the opposite of forcing patients to share records with each other; it protects each person's information from being shared with those who have no right to it.
ww.To set the price a hospital may charge f: Setting room prices is not a HIPAA task; the Privacy Rule protects health information and has no power over what a hospital charges for rooms.

rw: HIPAA gives patients the right to inspect and obtain copies of their records and to request corrections to errors, which is why they can ask for amendments.

ww.To keep records secret even from their o: Patients cannot keep records secret from their own doctors under HIPAA, since providers need the information for treatment, and the right is to access records, not to hide them from care teams.
ww.To see their records only after a court: HIPAA does not require a court order before patients see their records; patients generally have the right to access their own records on request, within set time limits.
ww.To delete any entry in their records tha: Patients can request corrections, but they cannot simply delete entries they dislike, since records must stay accurate and complete, and the provider decides whether to amend.

rw: Health equity means everyone has a fair and just opportunity to reach their best health, which requires removing barriers like poverty, discrimination and poor access to care.

ww.The number of beds in a hospital compare: Comparing the number of beds across hospitals is a capacity measure, whereas health equity is about fair opportunities for all people to be as healthy as possible.
ww.The money that owners of a hospital have: The money owners have invested is financial equity, a term from accounting, and it is a different idea from health equity, which concerns fairness in health outcomes.
ww.Everyone receiving exactly the same care: Equity is not the same as equality; giving everyone exactly the same care ignores differing needs, and health equity means fairness based on what people need to reach good health.

rw: A probationary period is an early time in a new job when the employer closely reviews performance and fit before deciding whether to confirm the person in the role.

ww.A permanent guarantee that the worker wi: A probationary period offers no permanent guarantee of the job; employment can end if performance is judged poor, so the claim of a permanent guarantee is incorrect.
ww.A time when employees cannot be paid whi: Employees on probation are still paid for their work; unpaid checking would break wage law, and probation only means their performance is under close review.
ww.A time when employees must work without: A probation period does not mean working without breaks; employees keep the normal rights to rest periods, and the term refers to review of performance and fit.

rw: Orientation is a program that introduces new hires to the organization, its policies, safety rules and workplace, which helps them settle in and work safely from the start.

ww.A yearly review of the pay of the staff: A yearly pay review is a compensation process for existing staff, and it does not apply to new hires, who are introduced to the organization during orientation.
ww.A test of job skills that new hires must: A skills test that must be passed first is a competency assessment or screening step, and orientation is an introduction rather than an exam for new hires.
ww.A trip to visit other hospitals for staf: Trips to compare other hospitals are benchmarking visits, not orientation, which acquaints new employees with their own organization, its policies and its workplace.

rw: Manageable workloads, support and recognition tackle the main causes of burnout, such as overload and feeling undervalued, so they are the actions most likely to reduce it.

ww.Ignoring complaints from staff about the: Ignoring complaints about workload leaves the cause of stress in place and makes staff feel unheard, so burnout grows and does not shrink.
ww.Removing all breaks during long shifts s: Removing breaks during long shifts increases fatigue and stress, which raises burnout and the risk of errors, and any extra work done is outweighed by these harms.
ww.Increasing hours without support so staf: Adding hours without support piles on strain and exhaustion, so staff are more likely to burn out and make errors, rather than finishing work faster.

rw: SWOT analysis reviews an organization's internal strengths and weaknesses along with external opportunities and threats, and it helps leaders form a strategy based on that view.

ww.A review of staff, work, orders and task: SWOT does not review staff, work, orders and tasks; those words only match the first letters, while the real terms are strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats.
ww.A review of suppliers, workers, owners a: Suppliers, workers, owners and traders form a made-up reading of the letters; SWOT is a planning method and not a list of groups connected to the hospital.
ww.A review of surgeries, wards, operations: Surgeries, wards, operations and treatments are invented words matching the letters; SWOT stands for strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats and is a strategic planning tool.

rw: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks, and any delay on it delays the whole project, so it sets the minimum time needed to finish.

ww.The list of the most costly tasks in the: The most costly tasks ranked by price is a cost ranking and not the critical path, which depends on task order and timing and not on how much tasks cost.
ww.The path that patients follow from the e: The route patients take from the entrance to a ward is a patient flow path, a different use of the word path, and it is not a project scheduling concept.
ww.The shortest route between two offices f: The shortest route between offices is a travel question, and the critical path in project work is about the longest sequence of linked tasks and not about commuting.

rw: Read-back verification means the receiver repeats a verbal order to the person who gave it to confirm it was heard correctly, which prevents medication errors from mishearing.

ww.Triage of patients by need: Triage sorts patients by urgency of need and has nothing to do with repeating an order back, so it is not the practice of confirming a verbal order.
ww.Upcoding of a bill claim: Upcoding means billing for a higher level of service than was given, which is a billing fraud issue and unrelated to a nurse repeating back a medication order.
ww.Capitation payment plan: Capitation is a payment plan in which a provider gets a fixed amount per patient, so it is a financing method and not a communication safety practice.

rw: Active listening helps staff understand patient needs and prevent errors, because careful attention and checking what was said reduces misunderstandings in care and instructions.

ww.Avoid asking patients questions at all: Avoiding questions would stop staff from learning what patients need, and active listening works the other way by encouraging attention and questions that bring out needs.
ww.Shorten visits at all costs for the day: Shortening visits at all costs is not the aim of active listening, which often takes some time but improves understanding and safety, so rushing would work against it.
ww.Replace the need for written records now: Written records remain necessary for legal, safety and continuity reasons, and listening carefully cannot replace documentation, so this claim overstates what active listening does.

rw: Meeting with both nurses to hear each side and look for a fair solution is the best first step, because it respects both and addresses the cause of the conflict.

ww.Assign the shift to the nurse who compla: Giving the shift to the nurse who complains least rewards silence instead of fairness and does not resolve the disagreement, so it is likely to cause resentment.
ww.Ignore the dispute and hope it goes away: Ignoring a dispute usually lets it grow and harms teamwork and coverage, so hoping it goes away is a poor first step for a manager.
ww.Post the dispute publicly so nurses take: Posting the dispute in public embarrasses the nurses, splits the team and harms trust, whereas a manager should handle the matter privately and fairly.

rw: Empathy means understanding and sharing another person's feelings, which lets caregivers connect with patients and respond to their emotional needs during care.

ww.Telling the patient not to be afraid of: Telling a patient not to be afraid dismisses the feeling and does not show understanding, so it is reassurance without empathy, which needs acknowledging the patient's emotions first.
ww.Ignoring a patient's feelings so as to s: Ignoring feelings to stay objective is detachment, which is the opposite of empathy, since empathy requires noticing and recognizing what the patient is experiencing.
ww.Feeling sorry in pity for another person: Feeling sorry for someone is pity, which looks down on the person, while empathy involves understanding and sharing the feeling and so is more connected and respectful.

rw: Nonverbal communication carries messages through body language, tone of voice and facial expression, and it often shows feelings that words do not, which matters when caring for patients.

ww.Messages sent by email without any attac: Email is written communication, a form of words, so sending an email, with or without attachments, is not nonverbal communication, which uses body language and expression.
ww.Messages sent in spoken words only, with: Spoken words only is verbal communication, and the description that excludes gestures describes the opposite of nonverbal communication, which relies on gestures, expression and tone.
ww.Messages that nobody can understand or m: Messages nobody can understand are simply unclear, not nonverbal; nonverbal messages like a smile or posture can be easily understood by others in many situations.

rw: BID comes from the Latin bis in die and means twice a day, so a patient takes the medicine two times during each day, usually morning and evening.

ww.Three a day: Three times a day is TID, not BID, and confusing them would give a patient an extra dose, since BID has the prefix bi meaning two.
ww.Four a day: Four times a day is QID, a separate abbreviation, whereas BID comes from the Latin bis in die, which means twice a day.
ww.Once a day: Once a day is written as daily or QD, and BID refers to two doses, since the prefix bi means two and not one.

rw: PRN stands for the Latin pro re nata and means as needed, so the patient takes the medicine only when a symptom such as pain appears, not on a fixed schedule.

ww.At bedtime: At bedtime is written HS or qhs, a different abbreviation, whereas PRN refers to giving medicine only when a patient needs it and not at a fixed time.
ww.Every morning: Every morning is a fixed daily schedule and PRN is the opposite, a flexible order, because PRN stands for the Latin pro re nata, meaning as the situation requires.
ww.Before meals: Before meals is written AC, a separate abbreviation tied to meal timing, while PRN is not tied to meals but to the patient's need for the drug.

rw: NPO stands for the Latin nil per os and means nothing by mouth, which is ordered before surgery or tests so that the stomach stays empty.

ww.Normal pulse noted: Normal pulse noted is not a standard meaning of NPO, and a pulse note would be written in the chart in a different way, such as with vital sign entries.
ww.Needs doctor order: Needs doctor order is invented; NPO is an instruction to the patient and staff about food and drink, and it does not ask for any additional order.
ww.No pain observed: No pain observed is not what NPO means; pain is recorded with a different notation, while NPO restricts eating and drinking before procedures.

rw: A medically necessary service is reasonable and needed to diagnose or treat a condition, and payers use this standard to decide whether to cover a service.

ww.Services offered to staff as a perk of t: A perk of the job for hospital staff is an employee benefit, not medical necessity, which describes a service needed for a patient's diagnosis or treatment.
ww.Services that a patient wants but which: A service with no medical basis fails the test of medical necessity, which requires services to be reasonable and needed, so insurers would deny it.
ww.Services offered for convenience only, w: Services offered for convenience only are not medically necessary, since they do not diagnose or treat a condition, and payers generally refuse to cover them.

rw: Wait time is the statistic that shows how long patients wait to be seen, which is often tracked in emergency departments and clinics to improve access and satisfaction.

ww.Stay length: Stay length measures how many days patients remain in the hospital and not how long they wait to be seen, so it is a different statistic.
ww.Readmissions: Readmissions count patients who return to the hospital soon after discharge, which is a quality measure and says nothing about how long they waited for care.
ww.Bed use rate: Bed use rate, also called occupancy, shows how much of the bed capacity is in use and does not measure the time patients wait to be seen.

rw: A health unit coordinator manages communication and paperwork on a hospital unit, such as handling orders, charts, phone calls and schedules, and so supports nurses and doctors.

ww.Performs surgery on patients in the oper: Performing surgery is done by surgeons in operating rooms, and a health unit coordinator is a nonclinical role that supports a unit, so this task is not part of the job.
ww.Performs lab tests on blood and tissue s: Lab tests on blood and tissue are done by laboratory technologists, not health unit coordinators, whose work is clerical and communication related on the nursing unit.
ww.Prescribes drugs to patients after a sho: Prescribing drugs is limited to licensed prescribers like physicians, and a health unit coordinator is a clerical role without the authority or training to prescribe medicines.

rw: Shredding or securely destroying paper records that contain patient information makes them unreadable, so it keeps the information private and meets HIPAA rules on proper disposal.

ww.Giving them to a patient's neighbor to t: Handing records to a neighbor to throw away exposes patient information to an unauthorized person, which breaks privacy rules, so it cannot be a compliant method of disposal.
ww.Throwing them in the regular trash bins: Regular trash bins let anyone retrieve discarded papers, and intact patient information in them would expose private data, so this does not meet HIPAA requirements.
ww.Leaving them in a pile in a hallway unti: Leaving records in a hallway puts patient information where visitors and others can read it, which is a privacy breach, and so it is not compliant disposal.

rw: A superbill lists the services, diagnoses and procedure codes for a patient visit, and the billing staff use it to prepare the claim for insurance.

ww.Ordering medicines for the pharmacy shel: Ordering medicines is a pharmacy purchasing task and uses purchase orders, whereas a superbill is a billing form that lists the services given to a patient.
ww.Telling a patient what the doctor ate fo: A superbill is a financial and billing document and has no place for personal details like what the doctor ate for lunch, which would be irrelevant to claims.
ww.Reporting staff attendance to the office: Staff attendance is reported through timekeeping or payroll records, and a superbill instead lists the services provided to a patient so insurance can be billed.

rw: A DRG system groups hospital cases that have similar diagnoses, treatments and expected resource use, so payers can pay a set amount for each group of cases.

ww.A group of doctors who share a clinic an: A group of doctors sharing a clinic and profits is a group practice, a different thing, and DRG is a classification and payment system for hospital stays.
ww.A group of nurses assigned to one ward f: A group of nurses assigned to a ward is a staffing team, and a DRG has nothing to do with staffing but with grouping cases for payment.
ww.A group of drugs that treat the same ill: A group of drugs that treat the same illness is a drug class, and a DRG classifies patient cases and not medicines, so this definition is wrong.

rw: Under a fixed DRG payment, a hospital whose cost is below the amount keeps the difference as margin, which rewards efficient care, while higher costs would mean a loss.

ww.The patient pays the difference to the h: The patient does not pay the difference to the hospital, because under a DRG the payer pays the fixed amount and the hospital bears the risk of its own costs.
ww.The hospital loses money on each stay th: The hospital would lose money only if its cost were above the fixed payment, but here the cost is below, so the stay produces a gain and not a loss.
ww.The hospital refunds the difference to t: The hospital does not refund savings to the payer, because the fixed payment is set in advance and the hospital keeps any amount left after covering its costs.

rw: IPPS is Medicare's system of paying hospitals a set amount per inpatient discharge, usually based on the DRG, so the payment does not depend on the cost of each stay.

ww.A system that pays insurers for the cost: IPPS pays hospitals, not insurers, and it does not reimburse insurers for care; it is Medicare's way of paying hospitals for inpatient stays.
ww.A system that pays doctors per visit onl: IPPS covers hospital stays by setting amounts per discharge, and paying doctors per visit only would ignore hospital stays, so this option describes the opposite of its purpose.
ww.A system that pays patients for staying: IPPS does not pay patients for staying in hospital; it pays hospitals for care provided, and a longer stay would not bring the patient any money.

rw: The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program is a Medicare program that cuts payments to hospitals with higher than expected readmissions for certain conditions, giving them a reason to improve discharge care.

ww.A program that pays hospitals more for e: The program lowers, not raises, payments for excess readmissions; paying more for each readmission would reward poor care and the program was designed to discourage that outcome.
ww.A program that builds new hospitals in t: Building hospitals in rural towns is not what this program does; it adjusts Medicare payments based on readmission performance and does not fund construction in areas that lack a hospital.
ww.A program that ends Medicare for all hos: The program does not end Medicare or move members to private plans; it is a payment adjustment for hospitals with excess readmissions, and Medicare continues unchanged for beneficiaries.

rw: Hospital value-based purchasing adjusts Medicare payments to hospitals using scores on quality and patient experience, rewarding better performance and giving poorer performers lower payments.

ww.Paying for the most services performed b: Paying for the most services is fee for service, which rewards volume and not quality, so it is the opposite of value-based purchasing.
ww.Buying supplies at the lowest price only: Buying supplies at the lowest price is a supply chain approach and is not value-based purchasing, which is a Medicare payment method tied to quality scores.
ww.Paying a fixed fee per patient whatever: Paying a fixed fee per patient whatever the care is capitation, which ignores quality scores, and value-based purchasing instead adjusts payments according to performance on quality measures.

rw: OPPS is Medicare's method of paying hospitals set rates for outpatient services, grouped into categories, so the hospital knows in advance what Medicare will pay for each type of visit.

ww.A method for paying insurers for care gi: Paying insurers for care to their members is not OPPS; the system pays hospitals, and insurers are payers, so this reverses who gets paid.
ww.A method for paying patients for their t: Patients are not paid for their time under OPPS; it pays hospitals for outpatient services, and a patient receiving care is the one being treated and not paid.
ww.A method for paying nurses for their wor: Nurses' pay comes from hospital wages and not from OPPS, which is a Medicare payment system for outpatient services and does not set pay for staff.

rw: The 340B program is a federal program that lets eligible safety-net providers, such as certain clinics and hospitals, buy outpatient drugs at discounts to stretch resources for low-income patients.

ww.A program that sets the price of all dru: 340B does not set the price of all drugs sold nationally; it gives discounts to eligible providers only, and other buyers and sellers are not covered by it.
ww.A program for patients to buy drugs onli: 340B is a program for eligible providers and not an online store for patients, who do not buy drugs through it from home.
ww.A program that bans discounts on all dru: 340B encourages discounts to eligible providers and does not ban them, so a program that forbids discounts on all drugs to hospitals contradicts what the program does.

rw: Charge capture records all billable services and supplies provided to a patient, so the provider can bill correctly and does not lose revenue from missed charges.

ww.Capturing criminals who break into a hos: Catching burglars is a security matter, and charge capture is a billing term meaning that all services given to a patient are recorded so they can be billed.
ww.Charging patients extra fees for each se: Charging extra fees is not what charge capture means; it is about recording services that were actually provided, not adding additional charges on top of them.
ww.Capturing images of patients for the rec: Photographing patients for the record is clinical imaging or identification, not billing, and charge capture refers to recording billable services and supplies and not capturing pictures.

rw: A claim scrubber is software that checks claims for errors, such as missing data or coding mistakes, before they are submitted, which lowers denials and speeds payment.

ww.A tool for sorting mail in the office of: Sorting mail is an office task and not what a claim scrubber does; scrubbers are software tools that review billing claims for mistakes.
ww.A cleaning machine that scrubs the floor: A floor-cleaning machine is housekeeping equipment, while a claim scrubber is billing software that checks claims, so the name's literal meaning is misleading here.
ww.A tool for storing records of patients i: Storing patient records in a cabinet is filing, and a claim scrubber is a software tool that checks claims for errors and does not store records.

rw: The denial rate is the share of submitted claims that payers refuse to pay, found by dividing denied claims by total claims, and it shows how clean the billing process is.

ww.The share of patients who refuse care af: Patients refusing care after hearing the price describes lost patients or financial barriers, and the denial rate instead measures the share of claims that payers refuse to pay.
ww.The share of beds that are empty on a gi: The share of empty beds is the vacancy rate, the opposite of occupancy, and it is a capacity measure that has no relation to denied claims.
ww.The share of staff who refuse shifts tha: Staff refusing shifts concerns staffing and scheduling problems, not claims, so it cannot be the denial rate, which measures payer decisions on submitted claims.

rw: Denial rate is denied claims divided by claims submitted, so 80 divided by 1,000 equals 0.08, or 8 percent, which shows the share of claims refused by payers.

ww.80 percent: Eighty percent would mean 800 of 1,000 claims were denied, but only 80 were, so this mistakes the count of 80 for a percentage.
ww.0.8 percent: Zero point eight percent would mean 8 denials out of 1,000 claims, but there were 80, so this puts the decimal in the wrong place.
ww.12.5 percent: Twelve and a half percent comes from dividing 1,000 by 80, which inverts the ratio; the denial rate is denied claims over total claims, which is 80 over 1,000.

rw: Net collection rate is the share of the collectible amount, after contractual adjustments, that the provider actually collects, which shows how well the billing office turns charges into cash.

ww.The share of staff who are paid on time: Staff paid on time is a payroll measure and unrelated to collections, since the net collection rate looks at how much of the collectible amount is actually collected.
ww.The share of patients who pay in cash wh: Patients paying in cash at the time of care is a point of service collection measure, and the net collection rate covers all collectible amounts, not just cash payments.
ww.The share of beds that are filled on a g: The share of beds filled is the occupancy rate, a capacity measure, and it tells nothing about how much of the money owed was collected.

rw: Net collection rate is collections divided by allowed charges, so 190,000 divided by 200,000 equals 0.95, or 95 percent, showing most of the collectible amount was received.

ww.50 percent: Fifty percent would mean only $100,000 was collected out of $200,000, but the practice collected $190,000, which is far more than half of the allowed charges.
ww.105 percent: A rate above 100 percent would mean more was collected than allowed, but 190,000 is less than 200,000, so the rate must be below 100 percent.
ww.10 percent: Ten percent would mean only $20,000 was collected, but $190,000 was, and 10 percent is closer to the amount uncollected as a share of allowed charges, which is really 5 percent.

rw: Gross revenue is the total billed charges at full prices, and net revenue is what the hospital expects to receive after contractual adjustments and other deductions, so net is lower than gross.

ww.Gross is smaller than net, because gross: Gross is not smaller than net; gross includes all charges at list prices, so it is the larger figure before deductions, and net comes after them.
ww.They are the same thing and mean the tot: Gross and net are not the same, because contractual adjustments and write-offs reduce billed charges, so the amount actually expected is lower than the amount billed.
ww.Net is before any billing has been done: Net revenue comes after billing and adjustments, not before billing, so it is not a figure from before any billing has been done by the hospital.

rw: A contractual adjustment is the difference between the provider's charge and the amount the payer has agreed to allow, which the provider writes off and cannot bill to the patient.

ww.A bonus paid by an insurer to a provider: A bonus from an insurer for sending many claims is not a contractual adjustment, which is a reduction in charges and not a payment to the provider.
ww.A tax on revenue that a hospital pays ea: A tax on revenue is paid to a government, whereas a contractual adjustment is a write-down of charges to the rate agreed in a payer contract.
ww.A fine charged to a hospital by a regula: A fine from a regulator is a penalty, and a contractual adjustment is not a fine but an agreed reduction below the charge, so it is not a punishment.

rw: The contractual adjustment is the charge minus the allowed amount, so 5,000 minus 3,200 equals 1,800, which is the amount the provider writes off under the contract.

ww.$3,200: The allowed amount of $3,200 is what the payer will pay, not the adjustment; the adjustment is the part written off, which is the charge minus the allowed amount.
ww.$1,600: One thousand six hundred dollars is half of the allowed amount and has no basis in the figures; the adjustment is 5,000 minus 3,200, which is 1,800.
ww.$8,200: Adding 5,000 and 3,200 gives 8,200, but the adjustment is the gap between charge and allowed amount, found by subtracting, so it cannot exceed the charge itself.

rw: Payer mix is the proportion of a provider's revenue or patients from each type of payer, such as Medicare, Medicaid and commercial insurers, which affects the average payment and financial health.

ww.A mix of buildings on the grounds of a h: A mix of buildings on a campus is a facilities layout and not payer mix, which concerns the sources of payment, such as insurers and government programs, and not the buildings.
ww.A mix of staff such as nurses, doctors a: A mix of staff types is the skill mix or staffing mix, which is about workers and not about the payers who pay for care.
ww.A blend of drugs that a pharmacy prepare: A blend of drugs prepared for one patient is a compounded medicine, and payer mix has no link to pharmacy preparation but to who pays for care.

rw: Medicaid typically pays less than the cost of care and uninsured patients often pay nothing, so a high share of them squeezes margins and creates financial pressure.

ww.Those patients use no services at all, s: Medicaid and uninsured patients do use services, often a lot, so claiming they use none is false, and their use creates real costs for the hospital.
ww.Those payers pay the highest rates of an: Medicaid pays below commercial rates and uninsured patients often pay little or nothing, so they are not the highest paying group, and the hospital does not profit from them.
ww.Those payers never send bills to the hos: Payers like Medicaid do process claims and send payments to hospitals, and uninsured patients can be billed, so saying they never send bills is inaccurate; the problem is low payment.

rw: Price transparency means rules requiring providers to make the prices of services publicly available, so patients and payers can see and compare costs before getting care.

ww.Hiding prices from patients until after: Hiding prices until after care is the opposite of price transparency, which asks providers to make prices known in advance so patients can compare and plan.
ww.A see-through bill printed on clear plas: A see-through bill on clear plastic mistakes the word transparency for a literal material, while price transparency means openly publishing what services cost.
ww.Setting prices by law, so that all hospi: Price transparency does not set one price by law for all hospitals; it only requires that existing prices be shown, and hospitals can still charge different amounts.

rw: A good faith estimate is the provider's estimate of expected charges for a service given to an uninsured or self-pay patient, which helps them know likely costs before the care.

ww.A guess made by the insurer about how mu: An insurer's guess about its own payment is an estimate of benefits, not a good faith estimate, which a provider gives to an uninsured or self-pay patient about expected charges.
ww.A bill sent after care that lists the ch: A bill sent after care listing the charges is an itemized statement, whereas a good faith estimate is given before the service and shows expected, not final, charges.
ww.A promise of payment by the patient, mad: A written payment promise from the patient is a financial agreement and not an estimate, since a good faith estimate comes from the provider and is not a patient pledge.

rw: Financial counseling helps patients understand their bills, explore payment options and apply for financial assistance, so that cost does not stop them from getting care or leave them with debt.

ww.Setting prices for services and drugs so: Setting prices for services and drugs is done by management and pricing committees, whereas financial counseling helps patients with bills and ways to pay for care.
ww.Giving legal advice to patients who want: Giving legal advice to patients who want to sue is the work of lawyers and has nothing to do with financial counseling, which deals with bills and payment help.
ww.Selling insurance plans to patients who: Selling insurance plans is a sales job done by insurers or brokers, while a financial counselor helps patients understand coverage and bills, not sell them plans.

rw: Worked hours per patient day links hours of staff time to patient volume, so it is used to compare staffing levels with the number of patients and judge staffing efficiency.

ww.Measuring profit in dollars for the whol: Profit in dollars is a financial result and is not measured in hours per patient day, which describes staffing input and not the profit of the unit.
ww.Counting parking spaces used by staff an: Parking spaces used are a facilities measure and have no connection to worked hours per patient day, which compares staff time with the volume of patient care.
ww.Measuring supplies used on a unit each m: Supplies used on a unit are tracked by a supply or cost measure, and worked hours per patient day measures labor input, not supplies consumed.

rw: Worked hours per patient day is 1,200 hours divided by 400 patient days, which equals 3, meaning the unit used three worked hours for each patient day of care.

ww.1,600: Adding 1,200 and 400 gives 1,600, but the measure is a ratio, so hours are divided by patient days and not added to them.
ww.0.33: Dividing 400 by 1,200 gives 0.33, which inverts the ratio; the measure puts hours on top, so it is 1,200 divided by 400.
ww.4,800: Multiplying 1,200 by 400 gives 4,800, but a rate per patient day needs division, since multiplying hours by days does not produce hours per patient day.

rw: Eight full-time employees count as 8 FTEs, and 4 half-time staff count as 0.5 each, which adds 2, so the department has 8 plus 2, or 10 FTEs.

ww.6: Six would ignore most of the full-time staff; 8 full-timers alone make 8 FTEs, so the total must be more than 8 when half-timers are added.
ww.12: Twelve is the headcount of employees, 8 plus 4, but FTEs convert part-timers to a fraction, and the 4 half-time staff count as only 2 FTEs in total.
ww.16: Sixteen would count each half-time employee as 2 FTEs, 8 plus 8, but a half-time worker is only 0.5 FTE, so the total is 10.

rw: Labor share of revenue is labor cost divided by revenue, so 6 million over 20 million equals 0.30, or 30 percent, showing how much of income goes to wages.

ww.14 percent: Fourteen percent has no basis in the figures; 6 divided by 20 is 0.30, and 14 percent of $20 million would be only $2.8 million in labor.
ww.3.3 percent: Three point three percent comes from a decimal slip; 6 divided by 20 is 0.3, which is 30 percent, so labor is a much larger share than that.
ww.70 percent: Seventy percent is the share of revenue left after labor costs, 14 out of 20 million, and not the labor share itself, which is the 30 percent that is spent on labor.

rw: A flexible budget adjusts its planned amounts to match actual activity levels, such as patient volume, which allows a fairer comparison between planned and actual costs.

ww.A budget that never changes once it is a: A budget that never changes once approved is a static budget, the opposite of a flexible one, which is designed to be adjusted when activity changes.
ww.A budget with no numbers in it at all, o: A budget with no numbers is not a budget at all, since budgets are financial plans in dollars, and flexibility refers to adjusting amounts, not removing them.
ww.A budget made by a gymnast for the team: The word flexible has nothing to do with gymnastics; a flexible budget is an accounting tool that changes with activity levels and has no link to a club's team.

rw: In a zero-based budget every expense must be justified from scratch for each period, starting at zero and not from last year's figures, which prevents old spending from carrying on.

ww.A budget that begins with last year's am: Starting from last year's amounts and adding a small percent is an incremental budget, the usual alternative, and it is not zero-based because it begins with past spending.
ww.A budget with no spending in it, so that: A zero-based budget does not mean spending nothing; it means each expense must be justified anew, and departments still spend money on needed activities after approval.
ww.A budget with no revenue in it, so that: A zero-based budget includes revenue and costs, and the zero refers to the starting point of justification, so a budget listing only costs with no revenue is not what the term means.

rw: A rolling forecast is updated on a regular schedule and always looks a set period ahead, such as twelve months, so it keeps planning current as time passes.

ww.A forecast of weather for the days of th: Weather forecasts predict the climate, but a rolling forecast is a financial planning tool, and the word rolling refers to updating, not to weather patterns.
ww.A forecast for one day only, made at the: A forecast for one day only would be a daily forecast; a rolling forecast looks a set period ahead and is updated regularly, usually over months or quarters.
ww.A forecast made once and never changed i: A forecast made once and never changed is a static forecast, the opposite of a rolling one, which is revised on a regular basis as new data come in.

rw: Days cash on hand shows how many days a hospital could pay its operating expenses using its cash, which is a key measure of liquidity and financial strength.

ww.The days between bills that a hospital s: The days between bills sent to patients describe a billing cycle, not days cash on hand, which measures how long cash can cover operating expenses.
ww.The days patients stay in the hospital a: Patient days in the hospital after an operation is length of stay, a clinical measure, and has no connection to cash or the hospital's ability to pay expenses.
ww.The days in a year that a hospital is op: The days a hospital is open to patients relate to its operating schedule, and days cash on hand is a financial measure of cash reserves relative to daily expenses.

rw: Days cash on hand is cash divided by daily cash operating expenses, so 30 million divided by 300,000 equals 100, meaning the hospital can pay expenses for 100 days.

ww.0.01 days: Zero point zero one days comes from dividing 300,000 by 30 million, which inverts the ratio; days cash on hand divides cash by daily expenses, not the other way around.
ww.30 days: Thirty days would be right only with daily expenses of $1 million, but daily expenses are $300,000, so 30 million covers more than 30 days of spending.
ww.9,000 days: Nine thousand days does not follow from dividing or multiplying these amounts sensibly; dividing 30 million by 300,000 gives 100, and 9,000 would be an extreme overstatement of the cash cushion.

rw: A hospital's bond rating is an assessment, from agencies such as Moody's, of its ability to repay debt, which affects the interest rate it pays when it borrows money.

ww.A rating of nurse quality as scored by p: Nurse quality scores from patients are patient satisfaction or quality ratings, and a bond rating instead assesses a hospital's ability to repay borrowed money, so this is a different kind of rating.
ww.A rating of beds in the wards of a hospi: Rating the number of beds is a measure of capacity, and a bond rating deals with creditworthiness and not the beds in the wards of a hospital.
ww.A rating of food quality in the cafeteri: Food quality in the cafeteria is a service rating at most, and bond ratings are about financial strength and the ability to pay back debt, not about meals.

rw: A hospitalist is a physician who focuses on caring for patients while they are in the hospital, handling their inpatient care instead of seeing them in an office.

ww.A hospital owner who holds the deeds to: A hospital owner who holds the deeds is a property owner, and the word hospitalist does not mean ownership but a physician who works in the hospital.
ww.A nurse who visits homes to give care to: A nurse who visits homes is a home health or visiting nurse, whereas a hospitalist is a physician who works mainly in the hospital and not in patients' homes.
ww.A person who lists hospitals in a direct: Listing hospitals in a directory is clerical work, and a hospitalist is a doctor, so the name's resemblance to the word list is misleading here.

rw: An intensivist is a physician who specializes in caring for critically ill patients in intensive care units, managing life support and complex conditions with a team.

ww.A physician who treats only skin conditi: A physician who treats skin conditions is a dermatologist, a different specialty, and has no particular role in intensive care for critically ill patients.
ww.A physician who studies the history of m: A historian of medicine studies the past, whereas an intensivist treats critically ill patients, so the role in this option is academic and not clinical.
ww.A physician who works in a pharmacy and: A physician working in a pharmacy filling orders would be a pharmacist, not an intensivist, who is a doctor caring for patients in intensive care.

rw: A case manager is a professional who coordinates a patient's care and services across providers and settings, helping the patient get what is needed and avoiding gaps or duplicate care.

ww.A manager of food services who oversees: Overseeing the kitchen and meals is the work of a food services manager, and a case manager coordinates patient care and not kitchen operations.
ww.A manager of equipment who tracks and re: Tracking and repairing equipment belongs to a biomedical or equipment manager, and a case manager deals with patients' care plans and services, not with machines.
ww.A manager of legal cases who handles the: Handling suits filed against the hospital is the job of legal counsel or risk management, whereas a case manager coordinates a patient's care and resources.

rw: Utilization review evaluates whether services are medically necessary and appropriate, often to decide coverage or length of stay, which helps control costs and prevents unneeded care.

ww.Reviewing food menus for patients on the: Reviewing food menus is a dietary department task, and utilization review concerns whether services are medically necessary and used appropriately, not what patients eat.
ww.Reviewing building plans for new wards a: Reviewing building plans is a facilities or planning task and has nothing to do with utilization review, which looks at how patient services are used.
ww.Reviewing staff uniforms for the nurses: Reviewing uniforms is a dress code matter, and utilization review examines the use of medical services, so it has no link to what staff wear.

rw: Discharge planning prepares a patient to leave the hospital with the follow-up care and services needed, such as medicines, home help and appointments, which lowers the risk of readmission.

ww.Planning a patient's admission to a ward: Planning a patient's admission to a ward is admission or bed assignment, which comes at the start of a stay, while discharge planning concerns the end of it.
ww.Planning staff vacations and leave for t: Planning staff vacations is a scheduling task for management and has no connection to patient discharge, which is about getting a patient safely out of hospital care.
ww.Planning meals for the patients and the: Meal planning for patients and staff is a dietary service matter, and discharge planning is not about food but about preparing a patient to leave the hospital.

rw: A care transition is a patient's move from one care setting to another, such as hospital to home, and good coordination at that point helps prevent errors and readmissions.

ww.A transition lens, a type of glass that: A transition lens is eyewear that darkens in sunlight, a pun on the word transition, and it has no meaning in healthcare delivery or patient movement.
ww.A change of hospital name after a merger: A change of hospital name after a merger is a branding change and not a care transition, which relates to patients moving between settings of care.
ww.A change of staff uniforms from one colo: A change of staff uniforms is a dress code matter, and a care transition involves a patient's movement between care settings, so it is not related to what staff wear.

rw: Social determinants of health are non-medical factors such as housing, income, education and neighborhood that influence health outcomes, and they often matter as much as medical care itself.

ww.Only the doctor's skill, with no other f: Doctor skill is only one part of health, and social determinants are factors outside medicine, so a claim that no other factor matters ignores housing, income and education.
ww.Only the prices of medicines, which deci: Medicine prices affect access but are not the defining set of social determinants, which include many conditions in which people live, and not only the cost of drugs.
ww.Only a person's genes, which are passed: Genes affect health, but social determinants are the conditions of daily life, not inherited traits, and saying only genes matter ignores the role of environment and income.

rw: A community health center is a nonprofit clinic giving primary care in underserved areas, often charging on a sliding fee scale based on income, so cost does not block care.

ww.A hospital for the wealthy only, which t: A community health center does not serve only the wealthy; it exists to serve people who are underserved, and it does not turn away patients who cannot pay.
ww.A research lab that studies diseases in: A research lab testing drugs on animals is a laboratory, not a clinic, and a community health center delivers primary care to patients in the community.
ww.A pharmacy chain that sells drugs and go: A pharmacy chain sells drugs and goods for profit, whereas a community health center is a nonprofit clinic delivering primary care and often serves people who are underserved.

rw: A rural health clinic is located in a rural area and serves patients there, and it may receive special Medicare and Medicaid payment, which supports access to care in small communities.

ww.A sports club where members train and pl: A sports club is for exercise and games, and a rural health clinic delivers medical care in rural areas, so the club has no healthcare function.
ww.A farm that treats animals such as cows,: A farm that treats animals is a veterinary or farming operation, while a rural health clinic treats people in rural areas, so animal care is not its role.
ww.A city hospital that serves people who l: A rural health clinic serves rural areas, not large cities, and its special payment rules are part of its definition, so a city hospital with none does not fit.

rw: A skilled nursing facility gives short-term nursing and rehabilitation care after a hospital stay, such as therapy and medical monitoring, helping patients regain strength before they return home.

ww.A home for healthy seniors who live on t: A home for healthy seniors who need no help is independent living, whereas a skilled nursing facility provides nursing and rehabilitation to people with medical needs.
ww.A school for nurses only, where students: A school for nurses is a nursing school, an educational institution, and a skilled nursing facility instead gives care to patients who need nursing and rehabilitation services.
ww.A hospital emergency room where patients: An emergency room treats major injuries at once, and a skilled nursing facility is not for emergencies but for ongoing nursing and recovery care after a hospital stay.

rw: Assisted living gives housing along with help for daily activities, such as bathing, dressing and medicines, to people who need some support but not full nursing care.

ww.A hotel for travelers who stay a few nig: A hotel is for travelers and does not offer help with daily activities or care, whereas assisted living combines housing with support for people who need some help.
ww.Hospital intensive care for patients who: Intensive care is a hospital unit for very sick patients, and assisted living is a residential setting for people who need some help with daily tasks.
ww.A school where children learn to read, w: A school teaches children and is education, not care, while assisted living is housing with help for older or disabled adults who need support with daily life.

rw: A rehabilitation hospital helps patients recover function after illness or injury, such as a stroke or a broken hip, through intensive therapy and care by a team.

ww.A hospital for tests only, with no beds: A hospital for tests only with no beds would be a diagnostic center, and a rehabilitation hospital has beds and treats patients to regain function over time.
ww.A hospital for surgeries only, where pat: A hospital for surgeries only is a surgical or specialty hospital, whereas a rehabilitation hospital focuses on helping patients recover function through therapy, and stays are often longer.
ww.A hospital for newborns only, where babi: A hospital for newborns only would be a neonatal or children's facility, and a rehabilitation hospital serves patients of many ages who need to regain lost abilities.

rw: An academic medical center is a hospital affiliated with a medical school, and it combines patient care, teaching of future clinicians and research, so it serves three missions at once.

ww.A school without patients, where student: A school without patients is a classroom institution, but an academic medical center treats patients and teaches in the same place, which this option leaves out.
ww.A medical supply store that sells beds,: A store selling beds and masks is a medical supply business and not an academic medical center, which delivers care, teaching and research and does not sell goods.
ww.A research firm that sells studies on he: A research firm selling studies is a commercial enterprise, and an academic medical center is a hospital tied to a medical school that also gives care and teaches.

rw: A trauma center is a hospital equipped to care for severely injured patients around the clock, with surgeons, imaging and operating rooms ready at all hours.

ww.A place for routine checkups and tests f: Routine checkups for people who are well take place in primary care offices, and a trauma center is equipped for severely injured patients who need urgent care.
ww.A mental health clinic only, where peopl: A mental health clinic gives therapy and drugs for the mind and is not a trauma center, which deals with serious physical injuries that need immediate care.
ww.A pharmacy where patients buy drugs and: A pharmacy sells drugs and goods and does not provide emergency care for severe injuries, which is what a trauma center is set up to do.

rw: A Level I trauma center is the highest level of trauma care, with comprehensive services available around the clock and with research and teaching programs as well.

ww.A care center for minor injuries, staffe: A center for minor injuries staffed by a nurse is closer to an urgent care or first aid station, and Level I is the highest level, not the lowest.
ww.A pharmacy where patients buy drugs and: A pharmacy sells drugs and goods and is not a trauma center of any level, so it cannot describe the highest level of trauma care.
ww.A clinic with one doctor who sees patien: A clinic with one doctor on weekdays cannot provide round the clock trauma care, so it falls far short of a Level I center with comprehensive services.

rw: A patient flow problem is a delay caused by bottlenecks in moving patients through triage, treatment and admission, which leads to crowding and long waits in the emergency department.

ww.A flood in the building that fills the h: A flood in the building is a facility emergency and not a patient flow problem, which concerns delays in moving patients through the emergency department.
ww.A broken lock on the door of the ER that: A broken lock is a security or maintenance issue, and a patient flow problem concerns the movement of patients through the department, not access to doors for staff.
ww.A shortage of paper for forms and charts: A paper shortage is a supply problem and could slow work, but patient flow refers to bottlenecks in moving patients through steps of care and not to supplies.

rw: Boarding means holding admitted patients in the ED because no inpatient bed is available, which crowds the department and delays care for new arrivals.

ww.Putting up wooden boards over the window: Putting wooden boards over windows is a weather precaution for buildings, and the term boarding in an emergency department means something different, namely patients held there.
ww.Admitting patients to ships that sail fr: Admitting patients to ships has nothing to do with emergency department boarding, which refers to admitted patients waiting in the ED for an inpatient bed.
ww.Discharging patients early from the ED t: Discharging patients early frees beds and is the opposite of boarding, in which admitted patients stay in the ED because inpatient beds are not available.

rw: Bed management coordinates patient placement and the availability of beds, matching admissions, transfers and discharges so that patients get a suitable bed quickly and flow is smooth.

ww.Selling beds to the public from the stor: Selling beds to the public is a retail activity and not bed management, which is the internal coordination of where patients are placed and when beds are free.
ww.Making beds only, with fresh sheets for: Making beds with fresh sheets is only part of housekeeping, while bed management is broader and coordinates patient placement and bed availability across the hospital.
ww.Cleaning mattresses only, along with oth: Cleaning mattresses is a housekeeping task that supports bed turnover, but it is only a small part of what bed management does, which is coordinating placement and availability.
